parsed.title: Dissecting StrikeStub: ClickFix PowerShell Malware and Modular RAT
KongTuke ClickFix comes for a Canadian treasure: Canada Dry
parsed.summary: KongTuke, a ClickFix operator, has been injecting a loader into five websites of one drinks company, including canadadry.ca, mottsclamato.ca, drinknestea.ca, hydratewithcore.com and drinkbai.com. Some sites serve the loader from their own domain via a planted WordPress plugin, while others load it from outside hosts. The loader first harvests visitors' cookies and token-like storage values, then shows a fake Cloudflare check that tricks users into pasting a command into the Windows Run box. That command connects to an FTP server whose greeting downloads and starts two files, vclreg.exe and vclx370.bpl. Two sites first loaded the code in July 2026, and all five still carried it on 10 November 2026. Defenders should audit WordPress plugins and injected script tags on these domains, and check for these files in %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Themes.

parsed.title: Exchange for breakfast: Turla’s Cereal tricks are not for kids
parsed.summary: Turla, a Russia-aligned APT group, is behind Cereal, a previously undocumented modular .NET toolset designed to run on compromised Microsoft Exchange servers for long-term cyberespionage. ESET found it at a Kazakh governmental organization and later at a Romanian one, where it targeted emails involving NATO and EU addresses. The toolset has no external command-and-control infrastructure, because the victim's own Exchange server receives commands through web paths that resemble legitimate Exchange traffic. Its CerealBox component hijacks existing transport agents in memory to collect messages with attachments, leaving no new agent in Exchange's configuration. Its use of unusual .NET techniques, such as native code execution before the runtime starts and abuse of the native image cache, sets it apart from most recent APT cases.

parsed.title: 4EverAble2Shell is already mining Monero on live N-central servers
parsed.summary: 4EverAble2Shell is an unauthenticated remote code execution exploit against N-able N-central that grants root, and it works against 2026.4 Hotfix 2 when the Legacy API is enabled. The attacker sends a crafted SOAP fault to the Apache Axis endpoint, causing a Java class to run a shell command built from attacker-supplied data. A Python script then escalates from the nable account to root by abusing N-central's own maintenance helper, and the root command installs a Monero miner with persistence. Researchers found 21 live N-central servers mining for the operator within hours of exploit publication, 19 of them already on the patched build. Defenders should check for the listed file, persistence, process and network artifacts, treat any hit as full compromise, and keep the Legacy API disabled until the fix is released.

parsed.title: How AI Revived a Stalled Attack on a U.S. Retailer
parsed.summary: Attackers targeting a U.S. retail organization in September 2026 switched from hand-typed commands to long, error-free PowerShell scripts after their initial attempts were repeatedly blocked. Symantec assesses with high confidence that AI assistance was involved, with comments in the scripts reading as a model's reasoning and timing suggesting a human operator relaying output to an AI tool. About 10 minutes after querying SolarWinds Orion, the attackers used its bundled RabbitMQ Erlang cookie to run commands on a second server. The attackers appear financially motivated, searching point-of-sale scripts for passwords, and their tools overlap with ShadowPad-associated loaders and a staging server from an earlier non-AI intrusion. The AI added speed and reliability rather than new techniques, and Symantec saw dozens of similar AI-assisted attacks, mostly in September 2026.

parsed.title: WFX Phantom: The GitHub Actions Secret Stealer That Deletes Its Tracks
parsed.summary: The wfx stealer is a CI secret-stealing script that attackers push into repositories using stolen GitHub tokens, including tokens issued to the Fly.io GitHub App and bot accounts. It collects all Actions secrets, runner process memory and cloud credentials, then tries to persist in AWS and Azure after rotation. The attacker reverts each commit and deletes the workflow run to cover its tracks. Thousands of repositories are affected, and the stealer has shifted from HTTP servers to Telegram-only exfiltration. Defenders should search for the listed commit messages and run-number gaps, rotate reachable secrets, remove cloud persistence, and block collection hosts and Telegram egress.

parsed.title: Compromised GitHub accounts push CI secret stealer to tens of thousands of repositories
parsed.summary: A threat actor used stolen GitHub credentials from November 10 to push a malicious workflow payload, named wfx-loot, into tens of thousands of repositories. The payload is a roughly 1,500-line shell script that steals GitHub Actions secrets, cloud credentials and AI provider keys from CI runners. It escalates to deeper cloud access and attempts to persist through forged status checks, AWS trust policy rewrites and Azure federated identity injection. Compromised accounts first opened probe pull requests, and at least 1,806 repositories show signs the payload ran, though the run logs were deleted. Defenders should assume every secret and cloud role available to affected workflows is compromised, and check for a missing run number on the attacker's commits.

parsed.title: Attackers turn NIKKE’s game launcher into malware
parsed.summary: Attackers abused the NIKKE game launcher, a signed and legitimate binary from Shift Up and Level Infinite, by remotely instructing it to download a payload through its server-pushed task channel. The payload was a Lua-based info stealer disguised as a log file containing LuaJIT bytecode, and it ran inside the launcher process without modifying any shipped binaries. It targeted saved browser passwords and cookies from Chrome, Edge and Opera, cryptocurrency wallet extensions, and developer secrets such as SSH keys, Git credentials and Kubernetes configs. Stolen data was sent through the launcher's existing telemetry channel, and the full run took under ten minutes. Bitdefender Advanced Threat Defense stopped the launcher before exfiltration on protected systems, and the delivery server was taken down. Defenders should watch for non-browser processes accessing credential stores and for oversized log files with LuaJIT headers.

parsed.title: APT StingyBasilisk: Malware is flowing through the pipes
The Enemy Within. Tracking LIMINAL PANDA and SilentAir through Mobile Networks
parsed.summary: Enea reports on LIMINAL PANDA, a China-nexus actor that abuses mobile operator interconnect networks, and on SilentAir, a newly identified state-level actor. LIMINAL PANDA uses GTPDoor, a Unix implant for covert command and control, and Enea found a new variant, GTPDoor v3, that operates over GTP-U traffic, which is harder to inspect. SilentAir generates SS7 and Diameter signalling attacks from compromised operator nodes, with Taiwan as its primary target and VIP political and government subscribers among its victims. Its tactics include location updates for call and SMS interception, and it sent silent SMS to confirm interception was active. Enea sees possible but unconfirmed links between the two actors. The key takeaway for defenders is to secure all interconnect protocols as untrusted and share visibility across them.

parsed.title: Attackers Use Autonomous AI to Target Semiconductor, Defense and Civil Society Sectors
parsed.summary: Chinese-speaking attackers tracked as CL-STA-1238 used the open-source AI penetration testing framework Cairn, paired with Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek models, to run 25 autonomous operations against at least 19 organizations in semiconductor, defense policy and civil society sectors. Operators supplied only a target and a goal, and Cairn planned and executed the intrusions on its own, with no attacker-imposed time limit. The attacks confirmed unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10 organizations, including exposed personal data, persistent administrator accounts and a modified standards-ballot document. Unit 42 assesses with moderate confidence that this is China-nexus intelligence collection. The report's key takeaway is that the exploited weaknesses were known, such as authentication bypasses, weak credentials and dated CVEs, so identity hygiene, attack-surface reduction and patching remain effective.

parsed.title: Luna Moth Returns, Re-Targeting Law Firms Through Access Tokens
parsed.summary: Luna Moth, also known as Silent Ransom Group, is a data-extortion group that is returning to law firms that likely did not pay its earlier ransom demands. Instead of deploying remote-management tools or malware, the group persuades victims during video calls, posing as IT support, to copy a Microsoft Graph access token from Microsoft 365 Copilot. The attackers then replay the token from their own infrastructure to bulk-download files within about an hour. Because the token was issued to a compliant device after MFA and Conditional Access checks, the activity appears to be the user's own. Defenders should enable Continuous Access Evaluation with strict location enforcement and verify unsolicited IT calls through known help-desk numbers.

parsed.title: T-SQL Being Abused to Deliver Malware on Compromised MS SQL Servers
parsed.summary: Attackers are abusing exposed Microsoft SQL Server instances with a Go-based payload, dllhost.exe, that scans IP ranges for open TCP port 1433 using an embedded Naabu scanner. The malware brute-forces logins with a list of usernames and about 2,700 predefined passwords, then runs T-SQL commands that enable xp_cmdshell and download additional executables. Those executables include an XMRig Monero miner disguised as a Microsoft Edge update and a Gh0st RAT variant that supports keylogging, screen capture, and remote shell access. The campaign uses scheduled tasks and Run key persistence to survive reboots. Defenders should restrict SQL Server exposure to the Internet and enforce strong credentials.

parsed.title: 0% GPU utilization: How SANSAR hides Linux cryptomining
parsed.summary: SANSAR is a Linux cryptomining orchestrator tracked by Elastic as REF3364 that manages CPU and GPU miners over Tor. The actor gained root after compromising an exposed Ray job agent that accepted unauthenticated job submissions, then deployed the toolkit across three Linux GPU hosts. A kernel rootkit hides selected processes, files and socket entries, while a modified NVML wrapper reports 0% GPU utilization and random temperature and power readings. A separate netns backdoor retrieves its controller address from an Ethereum smart contract and provides shell access without authentication. Defenders should verify who can submit jobs to GPU clusters and check whether GPU monitoring libraries have been modified.

parsed.title: Analysis of phishing and malicious apps distributed via smishing messages claiming to offer “Pi rewards”
parsed.summary: Smishing messages posing as "Pi Network 500π rewards" target Korean users, delivered via KakaoTalk notifications and SMS links. The campaign runs a three-stage phishing site that harvests 24-word wallet seed phrases, then account, password, and phone data, and finally pushes a malicious APK disguised as the Pi Network app. The Android malware, detected as Trojan.Android.SmsSpy, intercepts SMS and OTP codes, takes remote commands from a C2 server, and scans for 34 cryptocurrency exchange, payment, and wallet app keywords. It hides from analysis tools and resists removal by abusing device administrator rights. Hidden iframes on the phishing pages also load a WebKit exploit framework, linked to the Coruna kit, against iOS Safari users on versions 17.3 and earlier. Defenders should note that updating iOS to 17.4 or later mitigates the iOS exploit.

parsed.title: PHP2Shell Exploitation on Check Point Gateway
parsed.summary: Beginning October 30, 2026, an attacker scanned for and exploited unpatched Check Point Security Gateways' Mobile Access portals, using PHP2Shell for initial access and CVE-2026-123039 for privilege escalation to root. The first wave targeted Israeli organizations and included destructive activity, while a second wave on November 2 hit organizations in multiple countries and sectors without evidence of destruction. The attacker deployed PHP webshells, the persistent TSGA backdoor, and TSProxy, which intercepts networking functions in appliance processes. TSGA and TSProxy are modified variants of PhiliKit, previously linked to China-nexus UNC5221, though the report says attribution remains uncertain and could reflect a false flag or initial access broker role. The attacker moved to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left a politically themed note.

parsed.title: TypoPrompting: From AI Typos to Malware
parsed.summary: TypoPrompting is a delivery pattern in which typosquatted lookalike domains of 27 AI brands, including Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek and Perplexity, redirect mistyped visits to ClickFix lures, browser-hijacking malware and search-hijacking extensions. One Claude typo led through a traffic distribution system and a fingerprinting gate to a fake verification page that instructed Windows users to run a hidden PowerShell command fetched from a decimal-encoded IP address. Another route delivered Net Guard, a Microsoft Store-signed app whose hash matched the listing but which contains browser-hijacking code that can change the default search engine and run remote JavaScript. A third route led to a Chrome Web Store extension that overrides the default search provider with a third-party domain, and 17 of its 30 kit extensions remained listed with 972,000 declared users. Defenders should control browser-to-shell handoffs, web-delivered installer provenance and search overrides, and provide direct routes to approved AI services.

parsed.title: Hunting ClickFix Attacks: Deep Dive into One Trick Across Four Different Payloads
parsed.summary: ClickFix is a social engineering technique that tricks victims into pasting a command into the Windows Run dialog under the guise of a fake CAPTCHA or verification check. Researchers hunting in the wild found five unrelated campaigns using this same lure with widely varying payloads. One fake DMarket gaming-marketplace campaign used a Google-signed utility to exclude the entire C: drive from Microsoft Defender and delivered a previously undocumented RAT, dubbed CrashHandler RAT. A Stripe-based implant used api.stripe.com as a two-way command-and-control channel, which evades destination-based blocking. Another server delivered only a Calculator launcher, but its infrastructure remained live and could be changed to deliver malware at any time. Defenders should disable the Run dialog for standard users, monitor Defender exclusion changes, and watch for shells or mshta spawned by browsers.

parsed.title: SignDrop: Windows Zero-Day That Turns Microsoft's Own CLFS Mitigation Into a Privilege Escalation Path
parsed.summary: SignDrop is a local privilege escalation from a standard user to NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, published by the researcher MSNightmare on November 10, 2026, with no coordinated disclosure, CVE, or patch. It abuses Microsoft's CLFS authentication mitigation, forcing clfs.sys to create a signature file at an attacker-chosen path, which is then replaced with a payload DLL. The chain is triggered through Microsoft Defender's signature update RPC interface and uses no memory corruption, relying only on legitimate Windows subsystems. Howler Cell reproduced the full chain, obtaining a SYSTEM shell, and the researcher's claim that about 80% of Windows installations are vulnerable is unsupported. Disabling CLFS authentication is not a safe workaround, so defenders should focus on behavioral detections such as hid.dll creation in the ink directory and Defender RPC calls from outside the Defender service tree.

parsed.title: Beyond ValleyRAT: inside a China-nexus Silver Fox operation
Crafty Microsoft Teams Booking Flow Disguises Device Code Phishing
parsed.summary: Attackers disguised a device code phishing attack as a Microsoft Teams meeting-booking workflow, as observed by Huntress in mid-October against a construction-industry employee. The spear-phishing email impersonated a real senior vice president using a typosquatted domain, and multiple redirects, including Google short links, helped the email evade URL reputation checks. The phishing site silently started a Microsoft device-code sign-in and copied the resulting code to the clipboard as a fake "Booking Reference" when the victim clicked "Confirm Meeting." The victim then entered the code on Microsoft's real device-login page, which authorized the attacker's session. Huntress quickly contained the incident, and the report advises treating unexpected device-code prompts as suspicious, restricting device-code authentication, and enforcing phishing-resistant MFA.

parsed.title: 56 AWS API calls in 141 milliseconds: Inside an AI-run intrusion
parsed.summary: A CyberStrikeAI server, an open-source platform pairing LLM agents with offensive tools, used stolen credentials from eight AWS identities across four accounts between September 30 and October 16, 2026. The activity followed a familiar sequence: validating credentials, harvesting Secrets Manager values and EC2 user data, decrypting an SSM parameter, and sending a remote command. One role made 56 user data requests in 141 milliseconds, and the operator returned after a 14-day gap. Six detection rules each fired on only part of the activity, and all 78 alerts were medium or low severity, so only correlation by source IP linked them. The report recommends high-signal behavioral detections, flexible correlation windows, rotating exposed credentials and instance roles, and restricting access to EC2 user data.

parsed.title: Malware Must Die!: MMD-071-2026 - Linux/KinsingBot a bad-bad -designed botnet a while ago.. until recent.
parsed.summary: Linux/Kinsing is a Go-written ELF bot with remote command execution, coded by an actor called "nook" and linked to the SystemTen operator at medium confidence. It gets in through weak Redis authentication, reused SSH keys and a Pastebin-hosted installer script, then plants a tweaked XMRig miner. The bot also offers encrypted C2 tasking, a SOCKS proxy, an on-demand backdoor and mass-scanning. It kills rival miners and removes cloud security agents, then spreads by reusing trusted SSH keys. Defenders should harden Redis and SSH, audit cron entries and rotate keys after any compromise.

parsed.title: How Attackers Hide ScreenConnect in Windows Installers
SCKit Worm Installs Rogue ScreenConnect Clients and Session Cookie Relays Across Hundreds of Endpoints
parsed.summary: SCKit is a worm-like toolkit that abused attacker-controlled ScreenConnect clients and RMM+ extension access to push commands to hundreds of managed endpoints across Huntress customer organizations, affecting at least 288 hosts in the initial wave. The kit runs as SYSTEM, installs a rogue ScreenConnect client, and deploys a "RelayTrap" that takes over the legitimate client's connection slot and persists through a scheduled task. A stage aimed at technician workstations is designed to steal ScreenConnect session cookies and push payloads to every session a technician can reach, though Huntress has not observed a successful spread beyond the initial endpoints. The campaign exploited RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, which accepted a blank access key, and ConnectWise disabled the affected extensions and urged partners to upgrade to ScreenConnect 26.6.5 or later. Defenders should avoid interactive ScreenConnect sessions with suspected hosts, use out-of-band tools such as WinRM, and remove persistence before returning systems to service.

parsed.title: School Bomb Threats: Hudson Rock Finds Reported Sender Accounts in Infostealer Data
parsed.summary: Hudson Rock found infostealer-derived credential records for two university email addresses linked to threatening emails that disrupted Italian schools on November 11. The Egyptian address appears in a Vidar infection record dated October 1, 2021, which includes browser-saved passwords, including two for Microsoft authentication pages. The Taiwanese address appears in the AlienTXTBASE collection, with its data placed more than a year before the threats. Hudson Rock's findings do not confirm that these credentials were used to send the threats, and the sender identity remains unverified. The report's main takeaway is that exposure intelligence should trigger prompt account containment, credential replacement, and endpoint remediation.
